title: Medical devices: Regulatory listings do not prove replacement
desc: Provides a traceable AI-device inventory whose versions, publication delays and product classifications limit adoption or workforce conclusions.

kps.k: The cluster documents regulated medical AI, not evidence that AI outperforms or replaces clinicians.
kps.d: FDA’s AI-Enabled Medical Device List provides a regulatory inventory spanning 1995 to March 2026, with extensive radiology coverage and entries across other clinical panels. It establishes a longstanding, cross-specialty regulatory presence. The supplied material offers no comparative clinical outcomes, adoption rates or labour-displacement findings, and presents no competing positions on those questions.

kps.k: The inventory supports traceable research into regulatory decisions, but its entries are not counts of distinct products.
kps.d: FDA records decision dates, submission numbers, devices, companies, panels and product codes, provides downloadable data, and links submissions to approval, authorization or clearance information. Researchers can use these records to investigate regulatory history. Successive AutoContour versions illustrate why analyses must distinguish regulatory records from unique products; repeated entries do not constitute independent corroboration.

qs.a: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices (AI-Enabled Medical Device List) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Publication delays limit what absence from the list can establish.
kps.d: FDA updates the inventory periodically and defers authorized devices whose decision summaries remain unpublished during data collection. An omitted device therefore does not necessarily lack authorization. Analyses of regulatory activity should account for the inventory’s publication window rather than treat each edition as a complete contemporaneous record.

qs.q: AI-enabled medical devices that have received authorization but for which decision summaries have not been published within the data collection period will be incorporated into a subsequent update.

kps.k: Identifying LLM-enabled devices remains a prospective disclosure and classification task.
kps.d: FDA encourages sponsors to include appropriate information in public summaries to improve identification of AI-enabled devices, including LLM-based functionality in a future update. This recommendation gives sponsors a practical disclosure role; it does not establish that the current inventory systematically identifies LLM functionality or measures its prevalence.

qs.q: To facilitate the FDA’s development of methods to identify AI-enabled medical devices more easily, including identifying those devices incorporating LLM-based functionality in a future update of this list, sponsors are encouraged to include appropriate information in their public summaries.

vlens.an: The selected regulator source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by treating the FDA list as a traceable, periodically updated inventory of regulatory decisions rather than evidence of clinical superiority, adoption or clinician replacement. Its main reasons are methodological: authorized devices may be temporarily absent because decision summaries were not published within the collection window, and systematic identification of LLM functionality remains a future, disclosure-dependent classification task. There is no material internal disagreement in this professional voice because the curated evidence contains only the FDA source; its variation consists of complementary cautions about completeness and classification, not competing positions.

elens.an: The 2026 source supports the proposition by treating the FDA list as a traceable regulatory inventory rather than evidence that AI improves clinical outcomes, is widely adopted, or replaces clinicians. Its main contribution is methodological: the inventory can support research into authorization history, but entries may include successive versions of the same product, and publication timing means omission from a particular edition does not establish lack of authorization. It also identifies a classification limitation specific to emerging LLM functionality: systematic identification remains prospective and depends partly on sponsor disclosures. There is no substantive internal disagreement in the supplied period because only one source is included; the variation lies instead in the kinds of caution it supplies—publication-window limits, product-version duplication, and disclosure-dependent classification. These cautions reinforce rather than qualify away the cluster’s principal proposition.
